\chapter{The People Not Here}
\label{ch:ta-avarkal}
\hlchaptermodality{85}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about somebody who is not in the room, choosing between the familiar and respectful words, and I can say we in the two ways Tamil requires.}

From cold: the four third-person and we-words, the front letter that marks distance, and the question each choice answers.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[avaṉ / avaḷ]{\ta{அவன்} / \ta{அவள்} — the pair underneath the respectful word}

\label{lesson:TA-C85-avan-aval}



\begin{quote}
Say the respectful word for a person who is not here. Say whether it tells you anything about their sex. (It does not.)

Today's two words do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அவன்} and \ta{அவள்}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{அவன்}} — \emph{avaṉ} — \textbf{he} \textbf{\ta{அவள்}} — \emph{avaḷ} — \textbf{she}
\end{quote}

These are the plain, familiar words, and \textbf{\ta{அவர்}} was built on top of them: the lesson that taught \ta{இவர்} said so in passing, that it comes from \ta{இவன்} and \ta{இவள்} with the same \textbf{-\ta{அர்}} that makes \ta{நண்பர்} out of \ta{நண்பன்}.

So the ending you met on a word for \emph{friend} is the same ending that turns a familiar \emph{he} into a respectful \emph{that person}. \textbf{One suffix, three words, and it does the same job in all of them.}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: choosing between them}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{about} & \textbf{you say} \\
\midrule
a man, familiarly & \ta{அவன்} \\
a woman, familiarly & \ta{அவள்} \\
either, respectfully & \ta{அவர்} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The choice is about the relationship, not about the grammar.} \ta{அவன்} and \ta{அவள்} go with somebody younger, a close friend, a child — the people you would use the familiar \ta{நீ} with rather than \ta{நீங்கள்}. Reaching for \ta{அவன்} about a stranger or an elder lands the way the familiar \emph{you} would.

A learner in doubt is safer with \textbf{\ta{அவர்}}. Being a shade too polite passes without comment; the other direction does not.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ta{அவன்}, \ta{அவள்}
  \item which of the three words hides the person's sex
  \item which one you would use about somebody's grandmother
  \item the ending that \ta{அவர்} and \ta{நண்பர்} have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word is \emph{she}? (\textbf{\ta{அவள்}}.) Which is \emph{he}? (\textbf{\ta{அவன்}}.) Which one would you choose if you were unsure of the relationship? (\textbf{\ta{அவர்}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[avarkaḷ]{\ta{அவர்கள்} — they, and an ending hiding in a word you already say}

\label{lesson:TA-C85-avargal}



\begin{quote}
Say the polite word for \emph{you}. Look at its last syllable.

You have been carrying a plural ending around since chapter two without being told it was one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அவர்கள்}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{அவர்கள்}} — \emph{avarkaḷ} — \textbf{they}
\end{quote}

It is \textbf{\ta{அவர்}} with \textbf{-\ta{கள்}} on the end, and \textbf{-\ta{கள்}} is Tamil's plural. The same piece is sitting on the end of \textbf{\ta{நீங்கள்}}, which is why that word does double duty as a polite singular \emph{you} and a plain plural \emph{you}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{one} & \textbf{more than one} \\
\midrule
\ta{நீ} & \ta{நீங்கள்} \\
\ta{அவர்} & \ta{அவர்கள்} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The ending you have been pronouncing for eighty chapters turns out to be a word-building piece}, and now it builds something for you rather than arriving pre-attached.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same double duty}]
\textbf{\ta{அவர்கள்}} carries the same ambiguity as \ta{நீங்கள்}. About several people it is plainly \emph{they}; about one person it is a step more respectful still than \ta{அவர்} — the way some languages use a plural to raise the register.

Context settles which, and context usually settles it easily: a room with three people in it needs no disambiguation.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ta{அவர்கள்}
  \item the two pieces it is made of
  \item the word for polite \emph{you}, and point at the same piece inside it
  \item what \ta{அவர்கள்} can mean about a single person
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is Tamil's plural ending? (\textbf{-\ta{கள்}}.) What is \ta{அவர்கள்} built from? (\textbf{\ta{அவர்}} plus that ending.) Which other word you already say carries it? (\textbf{\ta{நீங்கள்}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nām / nāṅgaḷ]{\ta{நாம்} / \ta{நாங்கள்} — two words for \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{}, and you have to choose}

\label{lesson:TA-C85-naam-naangal}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for \emph{I}.

Now say \emph{we}. Tamil will ask you a question first, and English never has.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நாம்} and \ta{நாங்கள்}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{நாம்}} — \emph{nām} — \textbf{we}, counting the person you are talking to \textbf{\ta{நாங்கள்}} — \emph{nāṅgaḷ} — \textbf{we}, not counting them
\end{quote}

English has one \emph{we} and hides which it means. Tamil has two and makes you decide every time.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you mean} & \textbf{you say} \\
\midrule
you and me & \ta{நாம்} \\
me and them, but not you & \ta{நாங்கள்} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Shall we go?\textquotedblright{}} said to a friend is \textbf{\ta{நாம்}} — the invitation is the point. \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}We went yesterday\textquotedblright{}} said to somebody who stayed behind is \textbf{\ta{நாங்கள்}}, and using \ta{நாம்} there would tell them they had been present when they were not.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the piece you can already see}]
\textbf{\ta{நாங்கள்}} ends in the plural \textbf{-\ta{கள்}} met in the lesson before this one. \textbf{\ta{நாம்}} does not, and that is a useful shape to hold on to: the shorter word is the one that gathers everybody in.

\textbf{This distinction has no English equivalent to lean on}, so it is worth practising as a question rather than as a pair of words. Before saying \emph{we}, ask whether the person listening is inside it. The answer picks the word for you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ta{நாம்}, \ta{நாங்கள்}
  \item which one you would use to invite a friend somewhere
  \item which one you would use telling a friend about a trip they missed
  \item which of the two carries the plural ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which \emph{we} includes the listener? (\textbf{\ta{நாம்}}.) Which leaves them out? (\textbf{\ta{நாங்கள்}}.) What question do you ask yourself before choosing? (Whether the person listening is inside the \emph{we}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[avarkaḷ ninaivu]{(the people not here) — four words, from cold}

\label{lesson:TA-R85-avarkal-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the four lessons before this one. Say the word for \emph{this person}, the one you have had since chapter thirty-seven.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the table, filled in}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{near} & \textbf{far} \\
\midrule
respectfully & \ta{இவர்} & \ta{அவர்} \\
he / she & — & \ta{அவன்} / \ta{அவள்} \\
more than one & — & \ta{அவர்கள்} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The far column was empty and its pattern had been taught.} That is the shape of this chapter: the pointing system arrived long ago, correct and complete as a rule, with only half its cells ever handed over.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the question behind each choice}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{before you say} & \textbf{ask yourself} \\
\midrule
he or she & how close is this person to me \\
we & is my listener inside it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both questions are ones English lets a speaker skip. Tamil asks them every time, and neither has a safe default you can lean on forever — though a learner in doubt about the first is better off one shade too polite.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four words this chapter taught, from memory
  \item which front letter all but one of them carry
  \item which \emph{we} invites the listener along
  \item the plural ending, and two words you know that carry it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word is respectful and hides the person's sex? (\textbf{\ta{அவர்}}.) Which is \emph{they}? (\textbf{\ta{அவர்கள்}}.) Which \emph{we} leaves the listener out? (\textbf{\ta{நாங்கள்}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[toṭakka mariyātai]{(\ta{வணக்கம்}, \ta{நன்றி}, \ta{சரி} — and the how-are-you)}

\label{lesson:TA-R85-the-opening-courtesies}



\begin{quote}
Greet someone. Then say the one word that means \emph{fine}, \emph{correct}, and \emph{all right} at the same time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: two facts about Tamil courtesy}
Both of the opening words carry a claim the book made once and never returned to.

\textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}} is \textbf{native}. Neighbouring languages reached for a Sanskrit borrowing for the same bow; Tamil kept its own word and uses it across every setting, formal to casual. That is unusual enough in the region to be worth knowing.

\textbf{\ta{நன்றி}} is native too — built on the word for \emph{goodness} — and it comes with a pragmatic warning: among people who are close, saying thanks out loud can sound \textbf{marked}, a small distance opening where none was wanted. The word is correct; the question is whether the moment calls for it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: answering, and how few words it takes}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you mean} & \textbf{you say} \\
\midrule
yes & \textbf{\ta{ஆம்}} \\
no & \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} \\
fine, agreed, got it & \textbf{\ta{சரி}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ta{சரி}} is the one that does the most work, because it answers three different questions — \emph{is that right?}, \emph{will you?}, \emph{understood?} — with one syllable pair and no change.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange — how are you, both sides}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{நீங்கள்} \ta{எப்படி} \ta{இருக்கிறீர்கள்}?} — how are you, respectfully
  \item \textbf{\ta{நலம்}} — the answer, and the whole reply is \emph{nāṉ nalamāga irukkiṟēṉ}
  \item \textbf{\ta{எப்படி}} on its own — \emph{how}, the question word inside it
  \item \textbf{\ta{பரவாயில்லை}} — \emph{no problem}, and also the Tamil for \emph{you're welcome}
\end{itemize}

That last one is the pair worth holding: English keeps \emph{no problem} and \emph{you're welcome} apart, and Tamil hands you one phrase for both.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Page covered, both sides out loud.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the greeting, and say whether it is native or borrowed
  \item yes, no, and the agreeing word
  \item the whole how-are-you question, respectfully
  \item the answer, in full
  \item what you reply when somebody thanks you
  \item when saying thanks out loud might land badly
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which single Tamil phrase covers both \emph{no problem} and \emph{you're welcome}? (\textbf{\ta{பரவாயில்லை}}.) And what is the risk of thanking a close friend out loud?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[uṅkaḷ peyar eṉṉa?]{(\ta{உங்கள்} \ta{பெயர்} \ta{என்ன}?) — four words, and the one that is missing}

\label{lesson:TA-R85-the-name-exchange}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for \emph{my}. Then the word for \emph{what}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the sentence with no verb in it}]
\textbf{\ta{என்} \ta{பெயர்} …} is \emph{my name …}, and there the sentence stops. No word stands where English puts \textbf{is}.

That is not an abbreviation or a casual drop. Tamil \textbf{does not need a verb to link two things}: put the two nouns side by side and the link is understood. The same silence sits inside the question — \textbf{\ta{உங்கள்} \ta{பெயர்} \ta{என்ன}?} is \emph{your name what?}, three words doing what English needs four to do.

Once you have seen it here, you have seen it everywhere it happens.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange — both sides, end to end}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{move} & \textbf{what you say} \\
\midrule
ask & \textbf{\ta{உங்கள்} \ta{பெயர்} \ta{என்ன}?} \\
answer & \textbf{\ta{என்} \ta{பெயர்} …} \\
close it warmly & \textbf{\ta{மகிழ்ச்சி}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ta{மகிழ்ச்சி}} is worth its own moment: the word is \emph{joy}, and nothing more. It is not a built phrase meaning \emph{pleased to meet you} — it is one noun, offered, and the occasion supplies the rest.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the table. Take both parts.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the question, respectfully
  \item your own answer, with your name in it
  \item the warm word that closes a first meeting
  \item what \textbf{\ta{மகிழ்ச்சி}} means on its own
  \item where English would put a word that Tamil leaves out
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many words does Tamil need for \emph{what is your name?}, and which English word has no Tamil counterpart in it? (\textbf{Three; is}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pōy varugiṟēṉ]{(\ta{போய்} \ta{வருகிறேன்} — and the first four verbs)}

\label{lesson:TA-R85-going-and-doing}



\begin{quote}
Say the verb for \emph{go}. Then the verb for \emph{speak}.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ta{போய்} \ta{வருகிறேன்}} is what a Tamil speaker says on leaving, and it does not mean \emph{goodbye}. It means \textbf{I will go and come back}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you say} & \textbf{what it literally says} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{போய்} \ta{வருகிறேன்}} & I will go and come back \\
\textbf{\ta{மீண்டும்} \ta{சந்திப்போம்}} & we will meet once more \\
\textbf{\ta{நாளை} \ta{பார்க்கலாம்}} & tomorrow, let us see \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the right-hand column down and the pattern is unmistakable: \textbf{not one of the three names the parting}. Each one names the next meeting instead. A language can decline to have a word for goodbye, and this one does.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four verbs, two shapes}]
\textbf{\ta{போ}} \emph{go} · \textbf{\ta{பேசு}} \emph{speak} · \textbf{\ta{வாழ்}} \emph{live, flourish} — three plain stems. Then \textbf{\ta{வேலை} \ta{செய்}}, which is not one word but two: \emph{work} plus \emph{do}.

That second shape is worth naming, because Tamil uses it constantly. A noun parked in front of \textbf{\ta{செய்}} makes a verb out of it, which is how the language keeps borrowing things to do without borrowing verbs to do them with.

And \textbf{\ta{நான்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{பேசுகிறேன்}} shows what the stem does under pressure: \textbf{\ta{பேசு}} takes a tense piece and then a person piece, in that order, and the speaker is named at both ends of the sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover both tables.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all three farewells, and what each one literally promises
  \item the four verbs
  \item which of the four is built from a noun plus a doing-word
  \item \emph{I speak Tamil}, whole
  \item the two pieces that attach to a stem, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the everyday Tamil leave-taking literally say? (\textbf{I will go and come back}.) And which verb on this page is two words wearing one job?
\end{tcolorbox}
